abstract.objective: Meta-analysis of voxel-wise structural MRI studies reporting grey-matter differences between patients with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis and healthy controls.
inclusion_criteria: Empirical English-language structural MRI studies comparing patients with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or first-episode psychosis against a healthy control group.

The analysis must be VOXEL-WISE (VBM, voxel-based morphometry, SPM voxelwise). ROI-only or atlas/parcellation-only designs such as FreeSurfer region tables do NOT qualify, because they report per-region values rather than the stereotactic coordinates a coordinate-based meta-analysis requires.
exclusion_criteria: Reviews, meta-analyses, case reports, and single-patient studies.
Purely functional studies (fMRI, PET, MEG, EEG) with no structural morphometric outcome.
ROI-based or atlas-based-only morphometry with no voxel-wise whole-brain analysis.
Studies only of clinical high-risk or unaffected relatives with no patient-versus-control comparison.

inclusion.I1: Empirical English-language structural MRI studies comparing patients with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or first-episode psychosis against a healthy control group.
inclusion.I2: The analysis must be VOXEL-WISE (VBM, voxel-based morphometry, SPM voxelwise). ROI-only or atlas/parcellation-only designs such as FreeSurfer region tables do NOT qualify, because they report per-region values rather than the stereotactic coordinates a coordinate-based meta-analysis requires.

exclusion.E1: Reviews, meta-analyses, case reports, and single-patient studies.
exclusion.E2: Purely functional studies (fMRI, PET, MEG, EEG) with no structural morphometric outcome.
exclusion.E3: ROI-based or atlas-based-only morphometry with no voxel-wise whole-brain analysis.
exclusion.E4: Studies only of clinical high-risk or unaffected relatives with no patient-versus-control comparison.

exclusion_criteria: No stereotactic coordinates reported anywhere for a structural patient-versus-control contrast.

studies.title: Neuroanatomical abnormalities in first-episode psychosis across independent samples: a multi-centre mega-analysis.
studies.abstract: Neuroanatomical abnormalities in first-episode psychosis (FEP) tend to be subtle and widespread. The vast majority of previous studies have used small samples, and therefore may have been underpowered. In addition, most studies have examined participants at a single research site, and therefore the results may be specific to the local sample investigated. Consequently, the findings reported in the existing literature are highly heterogeneous. This study aimed to overcome these issues by testing for neuroanatomical abnormalities in individuals with FEP that are expressed consistently across several independent samples.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: The abstract describes a multi-centre mega-analysis of neuroanatomical abnormalities in first-episode psychosis but does not specify that voxel-wise (VBM/SPM) structural MRI methods were used or explicitly state a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison. Insufficient information to confirm I1/I2, so include for full-text review.
studies.fulltext_screening_reason: The full text reports MNI stereotactic coordinates and z-scores for regions showing grey-matter volume (GMV) changes (explicitly: “MNI coordinates and z scores for regions showing GMV changes in FEP relative to the HC”), indicating coordinates in a standard space for patient-versus-control structural contrasts. The neuroimaging analysis is a whole-brain voxel-wise VBM analysis implemented in SPM12/DARTEL with appropriate smoothing and whole-brain inference (FWE-corrected contrasts), satisfying whole-brain voxel-wise criterion. The patient group comprises first-episode psychosis participants meeting DSM-IV/ICD-10 criteria for schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (schizophrenia, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, etc.), so the clinical population is appropriate. Core article sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion) are present; supplementary materials/tables are referenced but not required. No exclusion criteria (E6–E8) apply.

studies.title: Morphometry and gyrification in bipolar disorder and schizophrenia: A comparative MRI study.
studies.abstract: Schizophrenia is believed to be a neurodevelopmental disease with high heritability. Differential diagnosis is often challenging, especially in early phases, namely with other psychotic disorders or even mood disorders. such as bipolar disorder with psychotic symptoms. Key pathophysiological changes separating these two classical psychoses remain poorly understood, and current evidence favors a more dimensional than categorical differentiation between schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. While established biomarkers like cortical thickness and grey matter volume are heavily influenced by post-onset changes and thus provide limited possibility of accessing early pathologies, gyrification is assumed to be more specifically determined by genetic and early developmental factors. The aim of our study was to compare both classical and novel morphometric features in these two archetypal psychiatric disorders. We included 20 schizophrenia patients, 20 bipolar disorder patients and 20 age- and gender-matched healthy controls. Data analyses were performed with CAT12/SPM12 applying general linear models for four morphometric measures: gyrification and cortical thickness (surface-based morphometry), and whole-brain grey matter/grey matter volume (voxel-based morphometry - VBM). Group effects were tested using age and gender as covariates (and total intracranial volume for VBM). Voxel-based morphometry analysis revealed a schizophrenia vs. control group effect on regional grey matter volume (p < 0.05, familywise error correction) in the right globus pallidus. There was no group effect on white matter volume when correcting for multiple comparisons neither on cortical thickness. Gyrification changes in clinical samples were found in the left supramarginal gyrus (BA40) - increased and reduced gyrification, respectively, in BPD and SCZ patients - and in the right inferior frontal gyrus (BA47), with a reduction in gyrification of the SCZ group when compared with controls. The joint analysis of different morphometric features, namely measures such as gyrification, provides a promising strategy for the elucidation of distinct phenotypes in psychiatric disorders. Different morphological change patterns, highlighting specific disease trajectories, could potentially generate neuroimaging-derived biomarkers, helping to discriminate schizophrenia from bipolar disorder in early phases, such as first-episode psychosis patients.
studies.abstract_screening_reason: Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study including schizophrenia patients vs. healthy controls and performs voxel-wise VBM whole-brain analysis (VBM/SPM), meeting the review’s inclusion criteria. studies.fulltext_screening_reason: The paper reports a whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis comparing schizophrenia (SCZ) patients and healthy controls using SPM/CAT12, with stereotactic MNI coordinates reported for a significant SCZ>control grey-matter cluster in the right globus pallidus at MNI [18 -2 5]. Methods describe voxel-wise, whole-brain analysis and multiple-comparison correction. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria I3 and I4; no exclusion criteria apply.

studies.title: A transdiagnostic neuroanatomical signature of psychiatric illness.
studies.abstract: Despite an increasing focus on transdiagnostic approaches to mental health, it remains unclear whether different diagnostic categories share a common neuronatomical basis. The current investigation sought to investigate whether a transdiagnostic set of structural alterations characterized schizophrenia, depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder, and determine whether any such alterations reflected markers of psychiatric illness or pre-existing familial vulnerability. A total of 404 patients with a psychiatric diagnosis were recruited (psychosis, n = 129; unipolar depression, n = 92; post-traumatic stress disorder, n = 91; obsessive-compulsive disorder, n = 92) alongside n = 201 healthy controls and n = 20 unaffected first-degree relatives. We collected structural magnetic resonance imaging scans from each participant, and tested for transdiagnostic alterations using Voxel-based morphometry. Inferences were made at p < 0.05 after family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons. The four psychiatric groups relative to healthy controls were all characterized by significantly greater gray matter volume in the putamen (right: z-score: 5.97, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 4.97, p-value = 0.001); the volume of this region was positively correlated with severity of symptoms across groups (r = 0.313; p < 0.001). Putamen enlargement was also evident in unaffected relatives compared to healthy controls (right: z-score: 8.13, p-value < 0.001; left: z-score: 9.38, p-value < 0.001). Taken collectively, these findings indicate that increased putamen volume may reflect a transdiagnostic marker of familial vulnerability to psychopathology. This is consistent with emerging conceptualizations of psychiatric illness, in which each disorder is understood as a combination of diagnosis-specific features and a transdiagnostic factor reflecting general psychopathology.

studies.title: Disassociated and concurrent structural and functional abnormalities in the drug-naïve first-episode early onset schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Schizophrenia which is an abnormally developmental disease has been widely reported to show abnormal brain structure and function. Enhanced functional integration is a predominant neural marker for brain mature. Abnormal development of structure and functional integration may be a biomarker for early diagnosis of schizophrenia. Fifty-five patients with early onset schizophrenia (EOS) and 79 healthy controls were enrolled in this study. Voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and functional connectivity density (FCD) were performed to explore gray matter volume (GMV) lesion, abnormal functional integration, and concurrent structural and functional abnormalities in the brain. Furthermore, the relationships between abnormalities structural and function and clinical characteristics were evaluated in EOS. Compared with healthy controls, EOS showed significantly decreased GMV in the bilateral OFC, frontal, temporal, occipital, parietal and limbic system. EOS also showed decreased FCD in precuneus and increased FCD in cerebellum. Moreover, we found concurrent changes of structure and function in left lateral orbitofrontal cortex (lOFC). Finally, correlation analyses did not find significant correlation between abnormal neural measurements and clinical characteristic in EOS. The results reveal disassociated and bound structural and functional abnormalities patterns in EOS suggesting structural and functional measurements play different roles in delineating the abnormal patterns of EOS. The concurrent structural and functional changes in lOFC may be a biomarker for early diagnosis of schizophrenia. Our findings will deepen our understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms in EOS.

studies.title: Increased Causal Connectivity Related to Anatomical Alterations as Potential Endophenotypes for Schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Anatomical and functional abnormalities in the cortico-cerebellar-thalamo-cortical circuit have been observed in schizophrenia patients and their unaffected siblings. However, it remains unclear to the relationship between anatomical and functional abnormalities within this circuit in schizophrenia patients and their unaffected siblings, which may serve as potential endophenotypes for schizophrenia.Anatomical and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were acquired from 49 first-episode, drug-naive schizophrenia patients, 46 unaffected siblings, and 46 healthy controls. Data were analyzed by using voxel-based morphometry and Granger causality analysis.The patients and the siblings shared anatomical deficits in the left middle temporal gyrus (MTG) and increased left MTG-left angular gyrus (AG) connectivity. Moreover, the left MTG-left AG connectivity negatively correlates to the duration of untreated psychosis in the patients.The findings indicate that anatomical deficits in the left MTG and its increased causal connectivity with the left AG may serve as potential endophenotypes for schizophrenia with clinical implications.

studies.title: Voxel-Based Morphometry Correlates of an Agitated-Aggressive Syndrome in the At-Risk Mental State for Psychosis and First Episode Psychosis.
studies.abstract: There are mixed reports on structural neuroimaging correlates of aggression in schizophrenia with weak evidence due to cohort overlaps and lack of replications. To our knowledge, no study examined volumetric neuroimaging correlates of aggression in early stages of psychosis. An agitated-aggressive syndrome is present in at-risk mental state (ARMS) and in first-episode psychosis (FEP) - it is unclear whether this syndrome is associated with structural brain abnormalities in early stages of psychosis. Using three-dimensional magnetic resonance imaging and a whole brain voxel-based morphometry approach, we examined 56 ARMS patients, 55 FEP patients and 25 healthy controls. We operationalized aggression using the Excited Component of the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS-EC) and dichotomized our patient group by median split into "BPRS-EC high" (n = 49) and "BPRS-EC low" groups (n = 62). The "BPRS-EC high" group had significantly smaller left lingual gyrus volume than HC. This finding was not present in the "BPRS-EC low" group. In addition, grey matter volume in the left lingual gyrus showed a negative linear correlation with BPRS-EC over all subjects (ρ = -0.318; p = 0.0001) and in the patient group (ρ = -0.202; p = 0.033). These findings provide first hints on structural brain abnormalities associated with an agitated-aggressive syndrome in ARMS and FEP patients.

studies.title: Common and distinct structural features of schizophrenia and bipolar disorder: The European Network on Psychosis, Affective disorders and Cognitive Trajectory (ENPACT) study.
studies.abstract: Although schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) share elements of pathology, their neural underpinnings are still under investigation. Here, structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) data collected from a large sample of BD and SCZ patients and healthy controls (HC) were analyzed in terms of gray matter volume (GMV) using both voxel based morphometry (VBM) and a region of interest (ROI) approach.

studies.title: Gray matter volume differences and the effects of smoking on gray matter in schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Many studies have evaluated differences in gray matter volume in schizophrenia, but have not considered the possible effects of smoking, which is extraordinarily common in people with the illness. The present study used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to examine differences in gray matter in subjects with schizophrenia and evaluate the effects of smoking on this measure.

studies.title: Medial prefrontal cortex pathology in schizophrenia as revealed by convergent findings from multimodal imaging.
studies.abstract: Neuroimaging studies have found evidence of altered brain structure and function in schizophrenia, but have had complex findings regarding the localization of abnormality. We applied multimodal imaging (voxel-based morphometry (VBM), functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) combined with tractography) to 32 chronic schizophrenic patients and matched healthy controls. At a conservative threshold of P=0.01 corrected, structural and functional imaging revealed overlapping regions of abnormality in the medial frontal cortex. DTI found that white matter abnormality predominated in the anterior corpus callosum, and analysis of the anatomical connectivity of representative seed regions again implicated fibres projecting to the medial frontal cortex. There was also evidence of convergent abnormality in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, although here the laterality was less consistent across techniques. The medial frontal region identified by these three imaging techniques corresponds to the anterior midline node of the default mode network, a brain system which is believed to support internally directed thought, a state of watchfulness, and/or the maintenance of one's sense of self, and which is of considerable current interest in neuropsychiatric disorders.

studies.title: Voxel-based gray and white matter morphometry correlates of hallucinations in schizophrenia: The superior temporal gyrus does not stand alone.
studies.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations (AVH) in schizophrenia (SZ) have been proposed to result from abnormal local, interregional and interhemispheric integration of brain signals in regions involved in language production and perception. This abnormal functional integration may find its base in morphological abnormalities. Structurally, AVHs have been frequently linked to abnormal morphology of the superior temporal gyrus (STG), but only a few studies investigated the relation of hallucination presence with both whole-brain gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) morphometry.

studies.title: Patients with poor response to antipsychotics have a more severe pattern of frontal atrophy: a voxel-based morphometry study of treatment resistance in schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Approximately 30% of schizophrenia patients do not respond adequately to the therapy. Previous MRI studies have suggested that drug treatment resistance is associated with brain morphological abnormalities, although region-of-interest analysis of MR studies from nonresponder and responder patients failed to demonstrate a statistically significant difference between these two schizophrenia subgroups. We have used a voxel-based analysis of segmented MR studies to assess structural cerebral differences in 20 nonresponder and 15 responder patients and 16 age-matched normal volunteers. Differences between the three groups emerged bilaterally mainly at the level of the superior and middle frontal gyri, primarily due to reduced grey matter volumes in nonresponders, as compared to both normal volunteers and responder patients. Post hoc direct comparison between the two schizophrenia subgroups demonstrated significantly reduced grey matter volumes in middle frontal gyrus bilaterally, in the dorsolateral aspects of left superior frontal gyrus extending into postcentral gyrus and in the right medial temporal cortex. Our results extend and integrate previous findings suggesting a more severe atrophy in nonresponder schizophrenia patients, compared to responder patients, mainly at the level of the superior and middle frontal gyri. Longitudinal studies in drug-naïve patients are needed to assess the role of these associations.

studies.title: Additive Effect of Cigarette Smoking on Gray Matter Abnormalities in Schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: It is widely known that there is a high prevalence of cigarette smoking in schizophrenia. One of the explanations is the self-medication hypothesis. Based on this hypothesis, it has been suggested that nicotine has procognitive effect or even neuroprotective effect in schizophrenia. However, cigarettes contain numerous neurotoxic substances, making the net effect of cigarette smoking on brain function and structure complex. Indeed, recent studies have called into question the self-medication hypothesis. We aimed to test whether there is an interaction between diagnosis and smoking status in gray matter volume, ie, whether smoking has specific effects on gray matter or whether main effects of these 2 variables additively affect common brain regions. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) images were obtained from 4 groups: (1) normal controls with no smoking history, (2) normal controls currently smoking and/or with a past history of smoking, (3) schizophrenia patients with no smoking history, and (4) schizophrenia patients currently smoking and/or with a past history of smoking. We used voxel-based morphometry to compare gray matter volumes among the 4 groups. We did not find any interaction between diagnosis and smoking, but we did find negative additive effects of schizophrenia diagnosis and smoking status in the left prefrontal cortex. The decrease in left prefrontal volume was associated with greater numbers of cigarette pack years and severe positive and negative symptoms. The current findings do not support the neuroprotective effect of smoking on gross brain structure in schizophrenia, emphasizing the necessity of longitudinal studies to test causal relationships among these variables.

studies.title: Finding specificity in structural brain alterations through Bayesian reverse inference.
studies.abstract: In the field of neuroimaging reverse inferences can lead us to suppose the involvement of cognitive processes from certain patterns of brain activity. However, the same reasoning holds if we substitute "brain activity" with "brain alteration" and "cognitive process" with "brain disorder." The fact that different brain disorders exhibit a high degree of overlap in their patterns of structural alterations makes forward inference-based analyses less suitable for identifying brain areas whose alteration is specific to a certain pathology. In the forward inference-based analyses, in fact, it is impossible to distinguish between areas that are altered by the majority of brain disorders and areas that are specifically affected by certain diseases. To address this issue and allow the identification of highly pathology-specific altered areas we used the Bayes' factor technique, which was employed, as a proof of concept, on voxel-based morphometry data of schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease. This technique allows to calculate the ratio between the likelihoods of two alternative hypotheses (in our case, that the alteration of the voxel is specific for the brain disorder under scrutiny or that the alteration is not specific). We then performed temporal simulations of the alterations' spread associated with different pathologies. The Bayes' factor values calculated on these simulated data were able to reveal that the areas, which are more specific to a certain disease, are also the ones to be early altered. This study puts forward a new analytical instrument capable of innovating the methodological approach to the investigation of brain pathology.

studies.title: FOXP2 expression and gray matter density in the male brains of patients with schizophrenia.
studies.abstract: Common genetic variants of FOXP2 may contribute to schizophrenia vulnerability, but controversial results have been reported for this proposal. Here we evaluated the potential impact of the common FOXP2 rs2396753 polymorphism in schizophrenia. It was previously reported to be part of a risk haplotype for this disease and to have significant effects on gray matter concentration in the patients. We undertook the first examination into whether rs2396753 affects the brain expression of FOXP2 and a replication study of earlier neuroimaging findings of the influence of this genetic variant on brain structure. FOXP2 expression levels were measured in postmortem prefrontal cortex samples of 84 male subjects (48 patients and 36 controls) from the CIBERSAM Brain and the Stanley Foundation Array Collections. High-resolution anatomical magnetic resonance imaging was performed on 79 male subjects (61 patients, 18 controls) using optimized voxel-based morphometry. We found differences in FOXP2 expression and brain morphometry depending on the rs2396753, relating low FOXP2 mRNA levels with reduction of gray matter density. We detected an interaction between rs2396753 and the clinical groups, showing that heterozygous patients for this polymorphism have gray matter density decrease and low FOXP2 expression comparing with the heterozygous controls. This study shows the importance of independent replication of neuroimaging genetic studies of FOXP2 as a candidate gene in schizophrenia. Furthermore, our results suggest that the FOXP2 rs2396753 affects mRNA levels, thus providing new knowledge about its significance as a potential susceptibility polymorphism in schizophrenia.

studies.title: Use of T1-weighted/T2-weighted magnetic resonance ratio images to elucidate changes in the schizophrenic brain.
studies.abstract: One leading hypothesis suggests that schizophrenia (SZ) is a neurodevelopmental disorder caused by genetic defects in association with environmental risk factors that affect synapse and myelin formation. Recent magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) studies of SZ brain showed both gray matter (GM) reduction and white matter (WM) fractional anisotropy reduction. In this study, we used T1-weighted (T1w)/T2-weighted (T2w) MRI ratio images, which increase myelin-related signal contrast and reduce receiver-coil bias.

studies.title: Decreased Gray Matter Volume of Cuneus and Lingual Gyrus in Schizophrenia Patients with Tardive Dyskinesia is Associated with Abnormal Involuntary Movement.
studies.abstract: Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a devastating motor disorder associated with the etiological process of schizophrenia or antipsychotic medication treatments. To examine whether cerebral morphological changes may manifest in TD, we used voxel-based morphometry to analyze high-resolution T1-weighted brain structural magnetic resonance images from 32 schizophrenics with TD (TD group), 31 schizophrenics without TD (non-TD group), and 32 healthy controls (HC group). We also assessed psychopathological symptoms with the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), and TD severity with the Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS). We compared gray matter volumes (GMVs) among groups, and tested for correlations between GMV changes and psychopathological symptoms or TD severity. The results showed significant differences in GMV in the frontal and temporal cortices, insula and cerebellum among the three groups. Brainstem and inferior frontal and precentral gyri GMVs were significantly larger, whereas cuneus and lingual gyrus GMVs were significantly smaller in the TD group as compared to non-TD group. Further, the cuneus and lingual gyrus GMVs were positively correlated with AIMS scores in the TD group. The current results suggest that TD may be associated with the alterations in GMV that are different from that of schizophrenics without TD. Further studies are needed to confirm and to examine the functional significance of these structural findings.

studies.title: Joint Coupling of Awake EEG Frequency Activity and MRI Gray Matter Volumes in the Psychosis Dimension: A BSNIP Study.
studies.abstract: Many studies have examined either electroencephalogram (EEG) frequency activity or gray matter volumes (GMV) in various psychoses [including schizophrenia (SZ), schizoaffective (SZA), and psychotic bipolar disorder (PBP)]. Prior work demonstrated similar EEG and gray matter abnormalities in both SZ and PBP. Integrating EEG and GMV and jointly analyzing the combined data fully elucidates the linkage between the two and may provide better biomarker- or endophenotype-specificity for a particular illness. Joint exploratory investigations of EEG and GMV are scarce in the literature and the relationship between the two in psychosis is even less explored. We investigated a joint multivariate model to test whether the linear relationship or linkage between awake EEG (AEEG) frequency activity and GMV is abnormal across the psychosis dimension and if such effects are also present in first-degree relatives.

studies.title: Progressive brain abnormalities in schizophrenia across different illness periods: a structural and functional MRI study.
studies.abstract: Schizophrenia is a chronic brain disorder, and neuroimaging abnormalities have been reported in different stages of the illness for decades. However, when and how these brain abnormalities occur and evolve remains undetermined. We hypothesized structural and functional brain abnormalities progress throughout the illness course at different rates in schizophrenia. A total of 115 patients with schizophrenia were recruited and stratified into three groups of different illness periods: 5-year group (illness duration: ≤5 years), 15-year group (illness duration: 12-18 years), and 25-year group (illness duration: ≥25 years); 230 healthy controls were matched by age and sex to the three groups, respectively. All participants underwent resting-state MRI scanning. Each group of patients with schizophrenia was compared with the corresponding controls in terms of voxel-based morphometry (VBM), fractional anisotropy (FA), global functional connectivity density (gFCD), and sample entropy (SampEn) abnormalities. In the 5-year group we observed only SampEn abnormalities in the putamen. In the 15-year group, we observed VBM abnormalities in the insula and cingulate gyrus and gFCD abnormalities in the temporal cortex. In the 25-year group, we observed FA abnormalities in nearly all white matter tracts, and additional VBM and gFCD abnormalities in the frontal cortex and cerebellum. By using two structural and two functional MRI analysis methods, we demonstrated that individual functional abnormalities occur in limited brain areas initially, functional connectivity and gray matter density abnormalities ensue later in wider brain areas, and structural connectivity abnormalities involving almost all white matter tracts emerge in the third decade of the course in schizophrenia.

studies.title: A New Division of Schizophrenia Revealed Expanded Bilateral Brain Structural Abnormalities of the Association Cortices.
studies.abstract: The phenomenological and, consequently, pathophysiological heterogeneity of schizophrenia may be substantially decreased by determining etiologically valid subgroups. In a cross-sectional study, we analyzed the brain structural impairments of outpatients with schizophrenia using concurrent subgrouping methods, partly to enhance the extensity of exploration, and partly to estimate the validation of the divisions. High resolution T1-weighted MR images were obtained for 21 patients and 13 healthy controls. Localized gray matter volumetric deficits were defined with optimized voxel-based morphometry. Employing two concurrent methods (i.e., the widely known deficit-non-deficit division vs. the neurocognitive clusters we identified earlier) the patient group was iteratively divided into two subgroups, and their volumetric peculiarities were compared with one another and with healthy controls. Our division revealed more significant differences demonstrating bilateral brain structural deficits, which affected the association cortices, primarily the heteromodal fields and partly the unimodal fields. This is the first study that showed that abnormalities of the association cortices can be bihemispherial and expanded in schizophrenia, even in the cases of outpatients living integrated in society. Our result suggests that the extended association cortex abnormalities could constitute substantial and determining neurological substrates in the phenomenology and aetiopathogenesis of schizophrenia, at least in a subgroup of patients with more unfavorable neurocognitive characteristics.

studies.title: Structural hippocampal anomalies in a schizophrenia population correlate with navigation performance on a wayfinding task.
studies.abstract: Episodic memory, related to the hippocampus, has been found to be impaired in schizophrenia. Further, hippocampal anomalies have also been observed in schizophrenia. This study investigated whether average hippocampal gray matter (GM) would differentiate performance on a hippocampus-dependent memory task in patients with schizophrenia and healthy controls. Twenty-one patients with schizophrenia and 22 control participants were scanned with an MRI while being tested on a wayfinding task in a virtual town (e.g., find the grocery store from the school). Regressions were performed for both groups individually and together using GM and performance on the wayfinding task. Results indicate that controls successfully completed the task more often than patients, took less time, and made fewer errors. Additionally, controls had significantly more hippocampal GM than patients. Poor performance was associated with a GM decrease in the right hippocampus for both groups. Within group regressions found an association between right hippocampi GM and performance in controls and an association between the left hippocampi GM and performance in patients. A second analysis revealed that different anatomical GM regions, known to be associated with the hippocampus, such as the parahippocampal cortex, amygdala, medial, and orbital prefrontal cortices, covaried with the hippocampus in the control group. Interestingly, the cuneus and cingulate gyrus also covaried with the hippocampus in the patient group but the orbital frontal cortex did not, supporting the hypothesis of impaired connectivity between the hippocampus and the frontal cortex in schizophrenia. These results present important implications for creating intervention programs aimed at measuring functional and structural changes in the hippocampus in schizophrenia.

Insufficient information to determine inclusion from abstract alone, so include for full-text review.

Exclusion E2: study is a purely functional imaging (fMRI) study with no structural morphometric outcomes. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a structural MRI study comparing structural measures), I2 (no voxel-wise structural analysis reported).

The abstract reports voxel-wise analyses of grey matter within patient samples (first-episode psychosis and chronic schizophrenia) but does not describe any patient-versus-healthy-control comparison. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I1 (no healthy control group reported). It does meet I2 (voxel-wise analysis). No exclusion criteria (E1–E5) are clearly met from the abstract.

Abstract describes an empirical English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing patients with schizophrenia to healthy controls (N=400). This meets I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria are evident from the abstract.

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing 99 DSM-IV schizophrenia patients to 113 healthy controls using voxel-based morphometry (VBM), satisfying I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, functional-only, reviews, non-human) are met or indicated. Full-text review appropriate to extract coordinates and details.

Abstract reports structural MRI in first-episode psychosis investigating brain volume reductions, but does not specify a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison nor whether a voxel-wise (VBM/SPM) analysis was used. Insufficient information to confirm I1 or I2, so include for full-text review.

Empirical structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia and early psychosis patients against healthy controls, and reports voxel-wise analyses (voxel-wise, subregion, and whole-thalamus scales). Meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria met; abstract provides sufficient evidence of voxel-wise morphometric testing relevant to the review.

Excluded because the study used a region-of-interest limited voxel-based morphometry approach rather than a whole-brain voxel-wise analysis (meets E3). Inclusion met: I1 (empirical structural MRI study comparing first-episode schizophrenia patients to healthy controls). Inclusion not met/demonstrated: I2 (voxel-wise whole-brain analysis) — abstract specifies ROI-only VBM.

This study reports an empirical structural MRI voxel-wise analysis (voxel-based morphometry) comparing patients with schizophrenia to healthy controls across two sites, satisfying I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Study uses voxel-wise VBM (SPM8) structural MRI comparing schizophrenia patients (n=31) to healthy controls and reports grey-matter differences; meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria apply from abstract. Recommend full-text review to extract coordinates and details.

Excluded because this is a functional MRI study (fMRI) reporting functional connectivity and signal aberrance, not structural morphometry—meets exclusion E2. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not a structural MRI study of grey-matter differences) and I2 (no voxel-wise structural/GMV analysis reported). No inclusion criteria satisfied. High confidence because abstract clearly describes functional imaging and connectivity analyses rather than voxel-wise structural MRI methods.

Empirical English-language structural MRI study of first-episode schizophrenia (n=34) vs healthy controls (n=36) using voxel-based morphometry (SPM99) with voxel-wise analyses and corrected voxel-level results; meets I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria apply.

Meets I1: empirical English structural MRI study comparing antipsychotic-naïve first-episode schizophrenia patients with healthy controls. Meets I2: performed voxel-wise analysis (VBM whole-brain). No exclusion criteria apply.

Exclusion E2: study uses neuromelanin-sensitive MRI and multimodal PET/fMRI to index dopamine function, not voxel-wise structural gray-matter morphometry. Inclusion criteria met: none (no evidence of voxel-wise structural MRI patient-vs-control analysis). Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (no demonstrated empirical VBM comparison of schizophrenia patients vs healthy controls), I2 (not a voxel-wise VBM/structural MRI study).

Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI case-control study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to compare schizophrenia patients with matched healthy controls, satisfying voxel-wise analysis requirement. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract.

Abstract reports GMV alterations in first-episode untreated schizophrenia but does not state whether a healthy control group was included or whether voxel-wise (VBM) analysis was performed. Inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are not demonstrably met from the abstract; full-text review needed to confirm methods and group comparisons.

Exclusion E3 met: study used a vertex-based (surface) cortical-thickness analysis rather than voxel-wise VBM/SPM. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no clear patient vs. healthy control comparison reported in abstract), I2 (analysis is not voxel-wise).

Study reports whole-brain VBM (I2 met) but compares genotype subgroups within patients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder and does not include a healthy control group, so it fails inclusion criterion I1. No exclusion criteria are clearly met.

Abstract reports voxel-based MRI analysis (satisfies I2) in first-episode psychosis patients but does not state a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison (I1 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria clearly met from the abstract. Full-text review needed to confirm presence of healthy control comparisons and availability of stereotactic coordinates.

Empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing first-episode schizophrenia patients to healthy controls and using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) and deformation-based morphometry (DBM), which are voxel-wise whole-brain methods. No exclusion criteria are met from the abstract. Full-text review recommended to confirm stereotactic coordinate reporting for coordinate-based meta-analysis.

Study reports empirical, English-language structural MRI with whole-brain voxel-wise VBM analysis comparing first-episode psychosis (FEP) patients (and ARMS) to healthy controls, matching the meta-analysis objective. Both inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are satisfied; no exclusion criteria apply.

Study uses diffusion tensor imaging of white matter in ultra-high-risk subjects and investigates WM integrity before/after onset. It is not an empirical voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI comparison of schizophrenia/first-episode patients vs healthy controls. Therefore inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are not met. No exclusion criteria E1-E5 are clearly met from the abstract.

Abstract reports gray-matter correlates in people with schizophrenia but does not specify whether a healthy control group was included or whether voxel-wise (VBM) methods were used. No exclusion criteria are clearly met from the abstract. Include for full-text review to determine voxel-wise analysis and patient-vs-control comparison.

Excluded (E3): ROI-only morphometric analysis; no voxel-wise whole-brain analysis reported. Inclusion met: none. Inclusion not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no patient vs healthy control comparison), I2 (no voxel-wise/VBM whole-brain analysis; manual ROI segmentation used).

Abstract reports structural MRI findings related to duration of untreated psychosis but does not specify whether a healthy control group was included or whether a voxel-wise (VBM) whole-brain analysis was used. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion criteria I1 and I2, so include for full-text review.

Title indicates a voxel-based morphometry study in first-episode psychosis, but abstract lacks explicit information confirming a patient-vs-healthy-control comparison required by I1. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Include for full-text review to verify presence of a healthy control group and voxel-wise coordinates.

Empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients (n=22) to matched healthy controls and reporting voxel-wise VBM analyses of grey matter volume (meets I1 and I2). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, review, non-human, or purely functional study) are evident from the abstract.

No evidence in abstract of voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI analysis. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met or not demonstrated: I1 (no clear patient vs healthy control structural MRI comparison reported), I2 (no voxel-wise VBM/SMP coordinate-based analysis reported; study focuses on white-matter/myelin integrity and PUFA concentrations).

Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients to healthy controls using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) (voxel-wise) and DTI to evaluate gray- and white-matter asymmetry, satisfying voxel-wise analysis requirement.

EXCLUDED: Does not meet inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met: I1 (study is DTI of white-matter, not structural T1-weighted MRI gray-matter morphometry), I2 (voxel-wise VBM/gray-matter analysis not performed). Not eligible for voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI meta-analysis.

Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI study including schizophrenia patients and healthy controls and explicitly uses voxel-based morphometry (VBM), satisfying voxel-wise analysis requirement. No exclusion criteria (e.g., review, purely functional, ROI-only) are met. Full-text review warranted to extract stereotactic coordinates and confirm patient illness stage and coordinates reporting.

Excluded because the sample consists of ultra-high risk (clinical high-risk) individuals rather than diagnosed schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis patients (E4). No evidence it included schizophrenia/FEP patients (I1 not met) and abstract does not report voxel-wise VBM analysis (I2 not demonstrated).

EXCLUDED: E4 (study only of clinical high-risk/unaffected relatives with no patient-versus-control comparison). Inclusion criteria met: I2 (voxel-wise VBM). Inclusion criteria not met: I1 — abstract reports high-risk familial subjects and within-group comparisons (converters vs non-converters), not a patient (schizophrenia/schizoaffective/first-episode) vs healthy control comparison.

Empirical longitudinal structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing first-episode schizophrenia (FESZ) patients with matched healthy controls, reporting voxel-wise grey matter differences and correlations with symptoms—meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria are met based on abstract.

Voxel-wise structural MRI study (DARTEL-based VBM) comparing 22 schizophrenia patients to 22 healthy controls; reports whole-brain grey- and white-matter voxel-wise differences and correlations, meeting inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

Excluded because study used manual tracing ROI-based GMV analysis rather than voxel-wise whole-brain morphometry (E3). Inclusion I1 is met (empirical structural MRI including first-episode schizophrenia vs healthy controls). Inclusion I2 is not met (no voxel-wise/VBM analysis; ROI-only manual tracing).

Study reports an empirical English-language structural MRI comparison of schizophrenia patients (n=45) versus healthy controls (n=42) using automated voxel-wise analysis (SPM/VBM) of whole-brain MRI. Meets I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria are apparent from the abstract.

Excluded because the study examined only high-risk relatives and healthy controls without a patient (schizophrenia/first-episode) versus control comparison, meeting E4. It used voxel-wise VBM analysis (I2 satisfied) but does not meet I1 (no patient group).

Study uses functional MRI (fMRI) to assess superior temporal lobe dysfunction; no structural voxel-wise MRI outcomes reported. Exclusion E2 applies. No inclusion criteria met: I1 (structural MRI) and I2 (voxel-wise structural analysis) not demonstrated.

Multisite voxel-based morphometry (VBM) study comparing first-episode and chronic schizophrenia patients to healthy controls, reporting voxel-wise structural MRI differences. Meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Exclusion E4 met: study uses a within-subject prospective design comparing participants before and after psychosis onset with no healthy control comparison. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no patient-versus-healthy-control comparison), I2 (voxel-wise analysis not stated in abstract).

The abstract reports a voxel-based morphometry (VBM) study of grey-matter volumes (I2 satisfied). However, it does not clearly state that the psychiatric patients are diagnosed with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder or first-episode psychosis, nor that patient-versus-control contrasts for schizophrenia are reported. Insufficient info to confirm I1, so include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

EXCLUDED because the study reports whole-brain white-matter morphology (VBM) in antipsychotic-naive first-episode schizophrenia rather than grey-matter differences required by this meta-analysis. Inclusion criteria met: I1 (empirical structural MRI patient vs healthy controls), I2 (voxel-wise VBM). Exclusion criteria met: none of E1–E5. Inclusion not demonstrated: reporting of grey-matter differences relevant to the review objective.

Abstract reports an empirical English structural MRI study using voxel-wise VBM (SPM8) comparing first-episode psychosis patients to matched healthy controls, meeting both inclusion criteria; no exclusion criteria apparent.

EXCLUDED: study uses voxel-wise VBM but reports white-matter volume differences rather than the grey-matter differences required by the review objective. Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I1 (contains schizophrenia patients vs healthy controls), I2 (voxel-wise VBM in SPM5). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: study does not report grey-matter differences (does not address the review's grey-matter outcome).

Abstract reports a whole-brain VBM (voxel-wise) study of schizophrenia patients with tardive dyskinesia, satisfying I2. However, the abstract does not state a patient-vs-healthy-control comparison, so I1 is not demonstrated. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Insufficient information to confirm inclusion, therefore include for full-text review.

E4 met: study includes only clinical high-risk (CHR) individuals vs healthy controls; no patient group with schizophrenia/first-episode psychosis. Inclusion met: I2 (voxel-wise VBM). Inclusion not met: I1 (does not compare patients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder or first-episode psychosis to controls).

Exclusion E2 met: this is a functional MRI (fMRI) language activation study with no structural morphometric outcomes. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 not satisfied (not an empirical structural MRI comparison), I2 not satisfied (not a voxel-wise structural/VBM analysis).

Abstract reports voxel-wise analyses in 15 schizophrenic patients correlating symptoms within patients but does not describe any comparison to a healthy control group. Thus it fails inclusion criterion I1 (no patient-versus-control comparison). It does meet I2 (voxel-wise analysis). No exclusion criteria (E1–E5) are clearly met from the abstract.

Study examines schizotypy in nonclinical subjects and does not report a patient (schizophrenia/schizoaffective/first-episode) vs healthy control comparison. Exclusion E4 applies. Inclusion I1 (patient vs control) is not met; inclusion I2 (voxel-wise structural MRI) is not demonstrated in the abstract. No inclusion criteria are satisfied.

Empirical structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing schizophrenia patients to healthy controls; matches inclusion I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria met from abstract (not a review, not ROI-only, not purely functional, human patients). Full text may be reviewed for coordinate reporting, but abstract supports inclusion for full-text review.

Exclusion E4: study examines unaffected siblings vs controls only, with no patient-versus-control comparison. Inclusion I2 is met (voxel-based morphometry). Inclusion I1 is not met (no patient group versus healthy controls).

Excluded because the study enrolled clinical high-risk (ARMS) youths rather than patients with schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or first-episode psychosis (meets exclusion E4). The study did perform voxel-based morphometry (I2 met), but I1 (patient diagnosis) is not met.

Excluded (E4): study examines ultra-high-risk (UHR) individuals versus healthy controls and does not compare patients with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis to controls. Voxel-wise analysis is reported (I2). Inclusion criterion I1 (patients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder or first-episode psychosis vs HC) is not met.

Exclusion E2 applies: this is a task-based fMRI (functional) study with no structural morphometric outcomes. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (structural MRI study) not met; I2 (voxel-wise structural MRI analysis) not met. Although it compares schizophrenia patients to controls, it does not report voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI results required for this meta-analysis.

Voxel-wise morphometric analysis (VBM/SPM) is reported, satisfying I2. The abstract does not report a healthy control comparison, so I1 is not demonstrated. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Because patient-vs-control status is unclear from the abstract, include for full-text review to confirm eligibility.

Abstract does not provide sufficient detail to confirm voxel-wise whole-brain analysis (I2) or explicit patient vs healthy control comparison (I1). No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Include for full-text review to determine whether VBM/voxel-wise methods and a patient–control comparison were performed.

Abstract compares schizophrenia patient subgroups (multiple vs fewer psychotic episodes) with no mention of a healthy control group (I1 not met). The abstract also does not state that voxel-wise whole-brain analysis (VBM/SPM) was used (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria (E1–E5) are clearly met from the abstract.

Abstract reports empirical structural MRI comparison between antipsychotic-naïve schizophrenia patients and healthy controls (I1). However, the abstract does not specify whether a voxel-wise whole-brain analysis (VBM/SPM) was performed (I2 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Include for full-text review to determine whether voxel-wise methods were used.

Exclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs met: I2 (voxel-wise VBM analysis reported). Inclusion IDs not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no empirical comparison of patients with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder/first-episode psychosis vs healthy controls is reported; study appears to be a genetic association sample of 72 subjects).

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients to healthy controls and reports voxel-wise regional grey-matter differences using voxel-based morphometry (VBM). Thus it satisfies I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria are met.

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI voxel-wise analysis (VBM) comparing schizophrenia patients (n=100) with healthy controls (n=264). VBM results reported and thus coordinates/voxel-wise analysis available. No exclusion criteria met in abstract.

Study reports voxel-wise whole-brain computational morphometry comparing psychotic patients and healthy controls, meeting voxel-wise analysis requirement. However the abstract does not explicitly state diagnoses (schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis), so eligibility is uncertain and full-text review is needed.

Abstract reports whole-brain voxel-based morphometric (SPM) analyses directly comparing childhood-onset schizophrenia patients to healthy controls, satisfying voxel-wise structural MRI requirements. No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to extract coordinates and details.

Abstract reports structural grey-matter findings in first-episode psychosis but does not specify whether there is a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison or whether voxel-wise methods (e.g., VBM/SPM) were used. No exclusion criteria are clearly met from the abstract. Include for full-text review to determine presence of voxel-wise analysis and a control group.

This article is itself a meta-analysis (E1). It is not an original empirical structural MRI study comparing patients versus healthy controls (I1 not met). Although it synthesizes voxel-wise VBM studies, the paper is not a primary voxel-wise analysis (I2 not met).

Excluded (E2): the study is a SPECT perfusion (functional) study with no structural MRI/morphometric outcome. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (not a structural MRI study) and I2 (no voxel-wise structural morphometry).

Exclusion criteria met: E2 (functional/MRS study without structural morphometric outcomes) and E4 (study of high schizotypy healthy subjects, not patients). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 (not an empirical structural MRI study of schizophrenia/first-episode psychosis patients vs controls), I2 (no voxel-wise structural MRI analysis).

Empirical structural MRI study that used voxel-based morphometry (VBM) on schizophrenia patients and healthy controls and examined gray-matter volumes (meets I1 and I2). No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not purely functional, not ROI-only, not high-risk-only, not non-human). Include for full-text review to verify voxel-wise patient-versus-control contrast coordinates for meta-analysis.

Structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing schizophrenia patients (n=20) to healthy controls (n=25), reporting voxel-wise GM differences; meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria apparent.

Abstract examines structural brain abnormalities in first-episode psychosis patients across ethnic groups but does not state whether a healthy control group was included nor whether a voxel-wise analysis (e.g., VBM/SPM) was performed. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Insufficient information to determine eligibility from abstract; include for full-text review.

Study reports an empirical English-language structural MRI comparison of schizophrenia patients (n=12) vs healthy controls and uses voxel-wise VBM whole-brain analysis; no exclusion criteria met (not a review, not ROI-only, not functional-only, human patients with controls).

Abstract provides insufficient information to confirm voxel-wise whole-brain analysis (I2) or a patient versus healthy control comparison (I1). Appears to be an empirical structural MRI study of adolescent-onset schizophrenia, but methods and control group not described—include for full-text review.

Title and abstract indicate an empirical English-language structural MRI study of early-course schizophrenia with voxel-based morphometry (VBM) assessing regional gray-matter differences versus controls. This satisfies inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria (reviews, functional-only, ROI-only, non-human, or high-risk-only) are evident from the abstract.

Empirical structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing 27 schizophrenia patients with 24 healthy controls. Meets I1 (patient vs control structural MRI) and I2 (voxel-wise VBM analysis). No exclusion criteria are met. Include for full-text review to extract coordinates and details.

The study uses optical coherence tomography (retinal imaging), not structural MRI voxel-wise analysis required. Inclusion I1 (structural MRI comparing patients vs controls) not met; I2 (voxel-wise analysis) not met. No exclusion criteria from the provided list are clearly met.

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing 41 schizophrenia patients with 42 healthy controls and explicitly states use of voxel-based morphometry (VBM), satisfying both inclusion criteria. No exclusion criteria are evident (not ROI-only, not review, not functional-only). Include for full-text review to extract coordinates and confirm voxel-wise results.

This is a within-patient longitudinal MRI study (pre/post atypical antipsychotic treatment) with no healthy control group, so inclusion criterion I1 is not met. The study does use VBM (voxel-wise) so I2 is satisfied. No exclusion criteria (E1–E5) are met.

Exclusion IDs met: E2 (purely functional study — fMRI) and E4 (study of unaffected first-degree relatives/genetic risk without patient vs control comparison). Inclusion IDs met: none. Inclusion IDs not met/demonstrated: I1 (not an empirical structural MRI study comparing patients with schizophrenia vs controls) and I2 (not a voxel-wise structural morphometry analysis).

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing medicated schizophrenia patients (n=69) with healthy controls (n=62) and explicitly states voxel-based morphometry (VBM) was used to investigate gray matter volume changes (voxel-wise). Meets I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria appear to apply. Include for full-text review to confirm stereotactic coordinate reporting and details.

Abstract describes structural MRI in first-episode psychosis but does not explicitly state a voxel-wise (VBM/SPM) whole-brain analysis nor a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison. Insufficient information to confirm key inclusion criteria (I1, I2); no exclusion criteria clearly met. Include for full-text review to determine voxel-wise methods and control group presence.

Excluded because the sample are adolescents at enhanced risk due to intellectual disability with no patient-versus-healthy-control comparison (Exclusion E4). Inclusion I2 (voxel-wise VBM) is met. Inclusion I1 is not met/not demonstrated.

Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry comparing patients with schizophrenia (and comorbid groups) against healthy controls, satisfying I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria apply (not a review, not purely functional, not ROI-only, not non-human).

Excluded (E4): study examined ultrahigh-risk subjects and compared converters versus non-converters with no patient-versus-healthy-control comparison. It used voxel-based morphometry (I2 satisfied) but did not meet I1 (no schizophrenia/first-episode patient vs healthy control group).

Study is a PET receptor-binding functional study (measuring dopamine D2/D3 binding during a task), not a structural MRI voxel-wise morphometry study. Exclusion E2 applies. Does not meet I1 (structural MRI patient vs control) nor I2 (voxel-wise structural analysis).

Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing schizophrenia patients (Kraepelinian and non-Kraepelinian) to healthy controls, meeting voxel-wise and patient-vs-control criteria; no exclusion criteria apparent from abstract.

Abstract reports cortical thickness and ANK3 effects in a first-episode psychosis sample but does not state a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison nor specify a voxel-wise whole-brain analysis. Because I1 and I2 are not demonstrated from the abstract, include for full-text review to determine eligibility.

Study compares schizophrenia patients (n=45) with matched healthy controls using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) to assess regional gray matter differences; meets voxel-wise structural MRI inclusion. Results report voxel-wise regional GM reductions correlated with quality of life. Sufficient information in abstract to include for full-text review.

Empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing antipsychotic-naïve first-episode schizophrenia patients to healthy controls using voxel-wise VBM (VBM8), meeting inclusion criteria I1 and I2.

Study reports voxel-wise structural MRI analyses (VBM and voxel-based cortical thickness) comparing first-episode psychosis patients to healthy controls, meeting the meta-analysis inclusion requirements.

Population is psychosis of epilepsy (POE), not schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder, or first-episode psychosis, so inclusion criterion I1 is not met. The study does use voxel-based morphometry (SPM99), satisfying I2. No exclusion criteria (E1–E5) are clearly met from the abstract. Excluded because the patient population does not match the review’s target diagnostic groups.

Study uses VBM on diffusion tensor MRI (DT-MRI) reporting white-matter FA differences, not voxel-wise grey-matter structural differences required for this review. Inclusion met: I1 (schizophrenia patients vs healthy controls). Inclusion not met: I2 (voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI results for meta-analysis) — DT-MRI/FA does not address grey-matter differences. No exclusion criteria (E1-E5) are directly met.

Abstract reports structural grey-matter volume comparisons between first-episode psychosis patients and healthy controls (satisfies I1) but does not specify that the analysis was voxel-wise (VBM). Insufficient information to confirm I2, so include for full-text review.

Excluded (E2): this is a functional EEG/LORETA source-imaging study (current density/P300) not a structural morphometric MRI voxel-wise study. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/demonstrated: I1 (not a structural MRI comparison of grey matter), I2 (not a voxel-wise VBM/SPM structural MRI analysis).

Empirical English-language structural MRI study of paranoid schizophrenia vs healthy controls using whole-brain voxel-wise analysis (optimized VBM). Thus it meets I1 (schizophrenia vs controls) and I2 (voxel-wise VBM). No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract reports an optimized voxel-based morphometry study of patients with schizophrenia and their siblings (meets I2). The abstract does not explicitly state a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison, so I1 is not confirmed from the abstract. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Include for full-text review to confirm presence of healthy control group and voxel-wise patient vs control coordinates.

Abstract does not report a voxel-wise structural MRI case-control comparison or stereotactic coordinates. It discusses structure and function related to insight in schizophrenia but lacks clear information on VBM/voxel-wise analysis and healthy control comparison. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Include for full-text review to determine whether I1 and I2 are satisfied.

Excluded under E4: study examines clinical/family high-risk groups (FR, CR, FRCR) versus controls with no diagnosed schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis patients. Therefore excluded from this meta-analysis focused on patient-versus-control studies.

Excluded (E4): sample comprises individuals at ultra-high/clinical high-risk for psychosis rather than patients with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis (I1 not met). Also study uses diffusion MRI (white-matter FA), not voxel-wise grey-matter structural MRI (I2 not met).

Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients to matched healthy controls and describes voxel-based whole-brain analyses of cortical thickness and GM volume density, consistent with voxel-wise methods required for coordinate-based meta-analysis. No exclusion criteria are met based on the abstract.

Abstract reports voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis of gray matter density comparing schizophrenia patients and healthy controls, satisfying inclusion criteria I1 and I2. No exclusion criteria are met in the abstract.

Empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients (n=29) to healthy controls (n=45) using a voxel-wise VBM approach (cerebellum-optimized VBM). Meets I1 and I2; no exclusion criteria evident. Include for full-text review to extract stereotactic coordinate data.

Abstract reports a voxel-based morphometry (VBM) whole-brain voxel-wise structural MRI study (meets I2). It does not explicitly state a patient-versus-healthy-control comparison (I1 not demonstrated). No exclusion criteria are evident from the abstract. Include for full-text review to confirm presence of schizophrenia patient vs healthy control comparisons and stereotactic coordinate reporting.

Title/abstract indicate structural MRI of treatment-naïve schizophrenia examining gray matter and DUP, but abstract does not specify a healthy control comparison nor that a voxel-wise (VBM) analysis was used. No exclusion criteria are clearly met. Insufficient information to confirm I1 and I2, so include for full-text review.

Exclusion E5: non-human study (transgenic rat). Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met: I1 — not a human patient vs. healthy control structural MRI study; I2 — not a voxel-wise VBM/coordinate-based analysis. Abstract reports an empirical English-language structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (VBM) comparing chronic schizophrenia patients against healthy controls; inclusion criteria I1 and I2 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply. Include for full-text review.

Excluded because this is a purely functional resting-state fMRI study with no structural morphometric outcomes (E2). The study does include a schizophrenia patient vs healthy control comparison (I1 met). It does not report voxel-wise structural MRI analyses (I2 not met).

Excluded for E2: this is a resting-state fMRI functional study reporting ALFF/fALFF, not structural morphometric outcomes. Inclusion criteria met: none. Inclusion criteria not met/not demonstrated: I1 (no clear structural MRI patient-vs-control comparison demonstrated), I2 (not a voxel-wise structural MRI analysis).

Empirical English-language structural MRI study comparing schizophrenia patients to healthy controls using voxel-wise VBM analysis on whole-brain gray matter; meets inclusion criteria I1 and I2 and no exclusion criteria are evident from the abstract.

No exclusion criteria met. Inclusion criteria met: I2 (voxel-wise VBM analysis). Study reports VBM correlations in 102 first-episode schizophrenia patients but does not report a patient vs healthy control comparison. Inclusion met: I2 (voxel-wise VBM). Inclusion not met: I1 (no patient vs healthy control group). No exclusion criteria clearly met.

Study used whole-brain voxel-based morphometry comparing 159 schizophrenia-spectrum patients to 158 healthy controls (meets I1 and I2). Abstract reports an empirical structural MRI study using voxel-based morphometry (voxel-wise) comparing recent-onset psychosis (including schizophrenia subgroup) to healthy controls, satisfying I1 and I2. fulltext_screening_results.reason: The full text reports MNI stereotactic coordinates and z-scores for regions showing grey-matter volume (GMV) changes (explicitly: “MNI coordinates and z scores for regions showing GMV changes in FEP relative to the HC”), indicating coordinates in a standard space for patient-versus-control structural contrasts. The neuroimaging analysis is a whole-brain voxel-wise VBM analysis implemented in SPM12/DARTEL with appropriate smoothing and whole-brain inference (FWE-corrected contrasts), satisfying whole-brain voxel-wise criterion. The patient group comprises first-episode psychosis participants meeting DSM-IV/ICD-10 criteria for schizophrenia-spectrum disorders (schizophrenia, schizophreniform, schizoaffective, etc.), so the clinical population is appropriate. Core article sections (introduction, methods, results, discussion, conclusion) are present; supplementary materials/tables are referenced but not required. No exclusion criteria (E6–E8) apply.

The paper reports a whole-brain voxel-based morphometry (VBM) analysis comparing schizophrenia (SCZ) patients and healthy controls using SPM/CAT12, with stereotactic MNI coordinates reported for a significant SCZ>control grey-matter cluster in the right globus pallidus at MNI [18 -2 5]. Methods describe voxel-wise, whole-brain analysis and multiple-comparison correction. Full text includes introduction, methods, results, and discussion and appears complete. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria I3 and I4; no exclusion criteria apply.

E6: The provided full text does not report any stereotactic coordinates (MNI or Talairach) for voxel-wise gray-matter contrasts between schizophrenia patients and healthy controls. I4 is satisfied: the study performed whole-brain voxel-wise VBM analyses in MNI space. I3 is not satisfied: no explicit coordinates or coordinate table are present in the supplied text (results describe regions and mention tables/figures but do not list x,y,z coordinates). Therefore the study cannot be included for a coordinate-based meta-analysis based solely on the provided full text.
